questions.trap_note: The default list is created ONCE at function definition, not per call — both calls share the same list. The obvious answer [1] then [2] is the trap.
questions.prompt: What does this print? Type the exact output (one line per print).
questions.code:
def f(x, items=[]):
    items.append(x)
    return items

print(f(1))
print(f(2))
questions.explain: Default argument values are evaluated once, when `def` runs. Every call that omits `items` reuses that same list object, so state leaks across calls. Fix: default to None and create the list inside.

questions.trap_note: Closures capture the VARIABLE, not its value at loop time. By the time any lambda runs, the loop is over and i is 2 — so the intuitive [0, 1, 2] is the trap.
questions.prompt: What does this print? Type the exact output.
questions.code:
funcs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in funcs])
questions.explain: All three lambdas close over the same variable `i`. They read it when CALLED, after the loop finished with i = 2. To freeze each value, bind it as a default: `lambda i=i: i`.

questions.prompt: `a == b` can be True while `a is b` is False, because `is` checks ______.
questions.answer: identity — whether both names point to the SAME object in memory (same id()) — while == checks value equality; two distinct list objects can hold equal values.
questions.explain: == calls __eq__ and compares values; `is` compares object identity (memory). Use `is` only for singletons like None.

questions.prompt: This function leaks items across calls — the asserts below fail. Fix it without changing its call signature's behavior for callers.
questions.asserts:
assert add_item(1) == [1]
assert add_item(2) == [2]
assert add_item(5, [1, 2]) == [1, 2, 5]
questions.explain: The None-sentinel pattern: a fresh list is created per call, and an explicitly passed list still works. This is the standard fix for the mutable-default pitfall.

questions.prompt: Complete the function: return a list of the squares of only the even numbers, in order.
questions.asserts:
assert even_squares([1, 2, 3, 4]) == [4, 16]
assert even_squares([]) == []
assert even_squares([7, 9]) == []
assert even_squares([0, -2]) == [0, 4]
questions.explain: One comprehension: filter (`if n % 2 == 0`) then map (`n * n`). Note 0 and negatives are even too — the asserts check the edge.

questions.prompt:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
b += [4]
print(a)

What does this print? (Trace it — every option is a real outcome of a wrong mental model.)
misconceptions: += rebinds b to a new list, leaving a untouched (true for tuples/str, not lists)
+= appends the list itself rather than extending
questions.explain: For lists, += is in-place extension (__iadd__): it MUTATES the shared object, so a and b — two names for one list — both show [1, 2, 3, 4]. With b = b + [4] instead, a new list is created and a would stay [1, 2, 3].
